I love running. I've been doing it since I was twelve when I took it up to turn from the fat kid in school into NCAA D1 5k & 10k meter runner, and now am a fun and fitness runner that sometimes does stupid things like ultra-marathoning. Whenever people ask me how to get into running this is what I tell them:

Commit to roughly ten hours spread over ten weeks and you'll be a long distance runner. It'll be terrible at first but by the end of ten weeks you'll probably love long distance running, and if you don't it's just not for you and there's probably nothing you can ever do to change that and just pick a different fitness hobby. I know on the surface this won't sound like it will make running more enjoyable for you, but hear me out, it will.

The hill repeat is the secret here. You want to find yourself a good repeat sprinting hill. Ideally this will be about 200-400 meters at a 10-15% incline, but you use what you've got that's convenient for you. If that's 4% incline for 100 meters, that's not ideal, but just use what you have that's convenient. Convenience so you don't have built in excuses to skip a workout is more important than your hill being perfect for these purposes. Same principle for distance. If you don't have a good way to measure your hill's distance just make a good guess and it'll be fine. If we were training for a specific length of event your specific length would be important, but for our purpose here it doesn't really matter that much.

Dedicate yourself to hill repeats twice a week. You are going to dead sprint up that hill for interval training. And I don't mean jog faster than you would on a long run, I don't even mean run, I mean sprint.

Sprint up the hill as fast as you can. When you reach the top, stop, turn around, and walk back down. As soon as you reach your starting point, you turn back around and repeat. You're not waiting at the bottom; as soon as you're at the starting point you're sprinting back up. Continue repeating this for twenty minutes. When twenty minutes have elapsed you're done. Your goal over the course of the ten weeks is to go from walking down the hill in a stumble, huffing and puffing, to walking briskly, to finally going down at a light jog; also you want to add a minute each week to have a repeat session of 30 minutes by the end. Your last week your aim is to be doing 30 minutes of repeats with a jog down the hill.

This workout is going to do several things. First, if you do it honestly without cheating yourself in a lesser effort it's brutal. Which sounds terrible, and kind of is. But the nice thing about running workouts is the harder they are the easier it is to get that legendary "runner's high" that marathon runners talk about. The "high" comes from two things: Endorphins that are released with all exercise and endocannabinoids, another type of chemical our bodies release during extended exercise (yes, they are called such because they have a similar effect as cannabis). You will get that high from this workout. An interesting thing about runner's high is that the more frequently you get it the easier it is to achieve and with stronger effects. You physically train your body to release the chemicals when it knows the muscles will need them, so the more often it happens the more efficient it becomes at the process. As such by the end of the ten weeks you will have basically given yourself an addiction to runner's high, and you will look forward to runs. Just to not midlead you, runner's high doesn't mean you'll feel just like you just spent an evening smoking pot, but you will feel great after a good run. It's like falling in love - hard to describe the specifics but you'll know the feeling the first time you get it.

The second thing about the workout being brutal is that all your other runs will seem so easy in comparison. I sort of lied about the one a hour a week thing, it's more like two hour. If you're going to become a runner you're going to want to run more than twice a week. But to start everything is built around those two hill repeat sessions a week, that one brutal hour. As a beginner you're aiming to run 4-5 days total a week, and don't worry about distance, just focus on time. On your non-sprinting days just aim to do 20-30 minutes at a casual pace (more than a light jog, but not a major effort). Those days will feel so easy compared to your sprint days you'll start to look forward to them. By the end of your ten weeks you will have trained yourself to like those type of runs, which are what most of long distance running is about.

The final aspect of this program is that you will make incredible gains in ability in a fairly short amount of time. Compared to someone who just decided to do the casual runs over ten weeks, your gains in speed and endurance will be vastly superior. Seeing how far you've come in a short period of time will be motivating, allowing you to experience first hand that no matter what point you started from you can become a good long distance runner. Obviously good is a relative term and some more than others, but you'll probably get much faster and stronger than you think you will be able to in only ten weeks from starting. Not to mention these are incredible fat burning workouts and you'll probably love the way you look too.

Once your ten weeks is over then you can move on to something else based on what you want to do. If you want to try your hand at a race pick your distance and search yourself up a training program. If you're just running for fun and fitness maybe you just dial back to one hill session a week swap the other for a long run day. You'll figure it out (hell, you could always @ me if you wanted some ideas). And later in your running career if you have no idea where else to go, the ol' hill repeat based program is that reliable tool that you can always go back to.

Good luck!
